text.p: Fluminense, relegated from the first division last weekend despite being one of the traditional giants of Brazilian soccer, say they want the rules changed to allow them to stay up.
The Rio de Janeiro club openly admits it wants to employ the age-old local practice of "turning over the table" -- tampering with tournament rules to favour some teams over others.
"Other teams have turned over the table in the past," Fluminense coach Renato Portulapp points out. "Why can't Fluminense do it?"
The club has the support of Dunshee de Abrantes, former president of fellow Rio club Flamengo.

"The clubs that will be promoted from the second division don't have the same traditions as Fluminense," he said. "It's important to turn over the table to prevent an injustice from being committed. It's morally right for Fluminense to stay up."

But the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) is eager to bring credibility to the domestic game and says Fluminense, who conceded 50 goals on their way to finishing 23rd in the 24-team division, must go down.

"Things are changing in Brazil and this applies to football as well," CBF director Gilberto Coelho said. "There is not the slightest possibility of turning over the table. We are a serious administration. The rules have been made and the bottom two teams will go down."
But doubts have been raised over the CBF's ability to withstand the pressure from Fluminense, who may appeal to the country's other big clubs for support.
Former Brazil international Gerson recently held up a piece of paper during a television interview and then tore it to shreds, saying: "This is what happens to the rules in Brazilian football."
And Tostao, Gerson's team mate in the 1970 World Cup winning team, added: "I have no doubt they will find a way of turning the table."
Brazil's leading soccer clubs have always looked on relegation as something that happens to other people.
For years, with up to 90 teams taking part in the national championship, it was never a real threat. More recently, with fewer clubs in the first division, it has become a reality.
Gremio, South American champions in 1983 and 1995, went down in 1991 and played in the second division the following season.

But in the face of pressure from other big clubs, the CBF ruled 12 sides would be promoted, facilitating Gremio's immediate return to the top flight and resulting in an ungamely 32-team first division in the next season.

Last year, the rules stated that if either of the two clubs finishing bottom had previously won the Brazilian championship, relegation would be decided by a play-off against the lowest-placed club never to have won the title. This year the rule was dropped.
If Fluminense are relegated, they will join Brazil's more modest clubs who face huge travel expenses as they criss-cross the continent-sized country to play in front of tiny crowds.
Second division matches are not televised and barely merit a mention in the Brazilian media.
